questions.stem: The four project phases in order are:
options: Identifying and defining → researching and planning → producing and implementing → testing and evaluating
questions.explanation: And it is iterative — findings from testing feed back into earlier phases. The process diary runs across all four.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest problem definition?
options: "Manual phone bookings take 6 minutes each and cause a 12% double-booking rate. We need an online system reducing handling time to under 1 minute with zero double-bookings, delivered in 12 weeks for under $15,000."
questions.explanation: It states the current state, the desired state, measurable success criteria, and the time and budget constraints — the anchor for every later decision.

questions.stem: A poor problem definition most directly causes:
options: Scope creep, the wrong solution and expensive rework
questions.explanation: The cost of an error grows by roughly an order of magnitude each phase it survives — a defect in the problem definition is the most expensive kind.

questions.stem: Defining scope requires stating:
options: Explicitly what is in and what is out of scope
questions.explanation: Naming exclusions is what makes scope enforceable in a later change-request conversation.

questions.stem: In SMART objectives, the "M" requires that an objective be:
questions.explanation: Measurable — Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. Without measurability there is no way to evaluate the finished system.

questions.stem: Which does a Gantt chart show that a simple task list does not?
options: Duration, dependencies, overlapping work, milestones and the critical path
questions.explanation: Bar length = duration, links = dependencies, diamonds = milestones, and the critical path is the sequence where any slip slips the whole project.

questions.stem: The critical path is:
options: The most expensive sequence of tasks
The longest chain of dependent tasks, which determines the minimum project duration
The tasks assigned to the most senior staff
The tasks with the most risk
questions.explanation: Tasks on the critical path have zero float — delaying any of them delays the project end date directly.

questions.stem: A PERT/network diagram is used primarily to:
options: Model task dependencies and compute the critical path and float
questions.explanation: It complements the Gantt chart: PERT emphasises the dependency network and slack; Gantt emphasises calendar time and progress reporting.

questions.stem: A work breakdown structure (WBS) decomposes:
options: The project deliverables into progressively smaller, assignable work packages
questions.explanation: It is the basis for estimating, scheduling and assigning — you cannot schedule work you have not decomposed.

questions.stem: Resource levelling addresses:
options: Over-allocation of a person or resource across concurrent tasks
questions.explanation: A schedule that assumes one developer works 160% of a week is not a schedule; it is a forecast of a missed deadline.

questions.stem: The process diary earns marks under EC-12-09 primarily through entries that record:
options: Decisions and their justification, problems encountered, solutions tried and reflections against criteria
questions.explanation: The "why" entries are the evidence of managed development and ongoing evaluation. A diary of "worked on the database" demonstrates nothing.

questions.stem: A project budget should include a contingency of approximately:
questions.explanation: 10–15% — is typical. The budget should also separate one-off build costs from ongoing operating costs, which are routinely forgotten and dominate lifetime cost.

questions.stem: The main benefit of an iterative approach over a single big release is:
options: Early and continuous user feedback, with risk surfaced while it is still cheap to fix
questions.explanation: The trade-off: harder to fix total cost and time up front, and it needs constant client availability.

questions.stem: The distinction between iteration and increment is:
options: Iteration adds features; increment removes them
Iteration refines the same thing; increment adds new pieces
questions.explanation: Agile does both — each sprint typically refines existing functionality and adds new capability.

questions.stem: "Follow-the-sun" development is an advantage of:
options: Offshore development across time zones, enabling round-the-clock progress
questions.explanation: The corresponding costs are communication friction, quality control, IP protection and data sovereignty when data crosses borders.

questions.stem: A significant data governance risk specific to offshore development is:
options: Personal data crossing borders into a different legal jurisdiction, engaging data sovereignty and cross-border disclosure obligations
questions.explanation: APP 8 governs cross-border disclosure — the Australian entity generally remains accountable for what an overseas recipient does with the data.

questions.stem: The most significant security concern with remote working is:
options: Home networks and personal devices sit outside enterprise security controls
questions.explanation: Mitigations: VPN, managed devices, MFA, endpoint protection, and clear policy on personal-device use.

questions.stem: The strongest worker-side criticism of gig/freelance arrangements is:
options: No leave, superannuation, sick pay or job security
questions.explanation: From the enterprise's side the trade-off is variable quality, availability risk, and knowledge walking out at project end.

questions.stem: Cloud IaaS/PaaS/SaaS most directly enables start-ups by:
options: Removing the capital expenditure barrier to infrastructure, converting it to operating cost
questions.explanation: Combined with open-source stacks, low/no-code tools, app-store distribution and online payments, a two-person start-up can reach the same customers as an incumbent — at the price of platform dependence.

questions.stem: Which is the most accurate statement about the effect of these changes on enterprise competition?
options: Barriers to entry have fallen, increasing competition, innovation and disruption — and also failure rates and platform dependence
Barriers to entry have risen sharply
questions.explanation: A balanced statement naming both sides is what an "analyse" or "discuss" verb requires.

questions.stem: The primary benefit of online collaboration tools for a project team is:
options: A single source of truth with version history and an audit trail of decisions, supporting asynchronous work
questions.explanation: Risks to name: tool sprawl, notification overload, access control and confidentiality, and dependence on connectivity.

questions.stem: In a system flowchart, a wavy-bottomed rectangle represents:
questions.explanation: Document — Also: trapezium = manual operation, cylinder = stored data/database, parallelogram = input/output, diamond = decision, oval = terminator.

questions.stem: A system flowchart differs from a program flowchart because it shows:
options: The whole system — manual and automated processes, hardware, storage media and document flows
questions.explanation: It is the artefact for showing a client how their business process actually runs end to end, including the human steps.

questions.stem: In a DFD, a process must:
options: Connect directly to another process only
Have at least one input and at least one output
questions.explanation: A process with input and no output is a black hole; output with no input is a miracle/grey hole. Processes are numbered and named verb + object ("1.0 Process Order").

questions.stem: A Level 0 (context) diagram shows:
options: All internal processes and data stores
The entire system as a single process with external entities and net data flows, and no data stores
questions.explanation: It establishes scope. Level 1 decomposes that single process into typically 3–7 processes and introduces data stores.

questions.stem: Balancing between DFD levels means:
options: The external entities and net flows crossing the system boundary are identical at Level 0 and Level 1
Each level has the same number of processes
questions.explanation: Level 1 only adds internal detail — it never invents a new external input or output.

questions.stem: Which is a DFD error?
options: A data flow directly from one data store to another
questions.explanation: Data must move through a process. Entity-to-entity flows are also errors, as are unlabelled flows.

questions.stem: In a DFD, data flows should be labelled with:
options: The name of the data moving
questions.explanation: "Booking request", not "sends booking". DFDs show where data goes, not when — sequence belongs on a flowchart.

questions.stem: Computational thinking in a project is best demonstrated by:
options: Deciding module boundaries, designing the database schema and writing the processing logic
Recognising the system changes rostering and accounting too
Producing an infographic for the public
questions.explanation: (A) is design thinking; (C) is systems thinking. Computational makes it work, design makes it usable, systems makes it fit.

questions.stem: Recognising that a new booking system will also change rostering, inventory, accounting and customer expectations is:
questions.explanation: Systems thinking — interdependencies, feedback loops, unintended consequences and lifecycle impact.

questions.stem: The correct order of the design thinking stages is:
questions.explanation: And it loops — test findings send you back to define or ideate. Low fidelity first: fail cheap.

questions.stem: In design thinking, empathise activities include:
options: Interviews, observation, surveys, personas and empathy maps
questions.explanation: Observation matters more than asking: users routinely describe what they think they do rather than what they actually do.

questions.stem: MoSCoW prioritisation stands for:
questions.explanation: It separates needs from wants and gives the client a structured way to trade scope against budget and timeline.

questions.stem: A RACI matrix documents:
options: Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each activity
questions.explanation: Exactly one person should be Accountable for each activity — shared accountability is no accountability.

questions.stem: The best way to prevent scope creep is:
options: Get a signed problem definition and scope, then run all changes through a documented change-request process with cost and time impact
questions.explanation: Change is legitimate; undocumented, unpriced change is what kills projects.

questions.stem: "Designing for ease of operation and maintenance" matters because:
options: Maintenance is the smallest lifetime cost
Maintenance is typically the largest lifetime cost, so modularity, documentation and clear naming reduce total cost of ownership
It removes the need for training
questions.explanation: The build is a fraction of the lifecycle. Configuration separated from code, logging, error handling and sensible defaults all pay off over years.

questions.stem: Which requirements-gathering tool best uncovers needs users cannot articulate?
questions.explanation: Prototype — Users react far more usefully to something concrete than to an abstract question. Risk: they mistake it for a finished product, or fixate on visuals over function.

questions.stem: The main limitation of surveys for requirements gathering is:
options: They are shallow — no follow-up questions, and poorly worded items bias results
questions.explanation: Surveys buy breadth and quantification; interviews buy depth and context. Using both is the strong answer.

questions.stem: Analytical reports from existing system data are valuable because they:
options: Explain why users behave as they do
Are objective, based on actual behaviour, and impose no burden on participants
questions.explanation: Their limitation is precisely (A) — they tell you what happened, not why, and the data may have been defined for another purpose.

questions.stem: Waterfall is most defensible when:
options: The client is unavailable and requirements are unclear
Requirements are stable and fully known, and the project is regulated, safety-critical or fixed-price
The team wants to deliver working software every two weeks
questions.explanation: In one line: waterfall buys certainty of cost and scope at the price of flexibility; agile buys flexibility at the price of certainty.

questions.stem: The greatest risk of agile for a fixed-price contract is:
options: Difficulty fixing scope, cost and date up front
questions.explanation: Agile also requires constant client availability and a skilled, self-organising team — both are real prerequisites, not optional extras.

questions.stem: Throwaway prototyping differs from evolutionary prototyping because:
options: The throwaway prototype is discarded and the system rebuilt properly; the evolutionary prototype becomes the product
Throwaway prototypes are never shown to users
questions.explanation: The risk of evolutionary prototyping is architectural debt — a proof of concept quietly becomes production without ever being engineered for it.

questions.stem: The characteristic risk of end-user development is:
options: Weak security, validation and backup, no version control, and key-person dependency when the builder leaves
questions.explanation: "Shadow IT" — the critical spreadsheet nobody in IT knows exists — is the classic manifestation.

questions.stem: The most significant long-term risk of outsourcing a core system is:
options: Loss of internal knowledge and control, plus vendor lock-in and ongoing licence dependency
questions.explanation: Outsourcing is a strong choice for non-core systems where no internal capability exists; it is riskier the closer the system sits to competitive advantage.

questions.stem: A storyboard in an implementation plan communicates:
options: The user journey and screen flow frame by frame, exposing missing steps to non-technical stakeholders
questions.explanation: It is the artefact that surfaces "wait — what happens if they don't have an account?" before any code is written.

questions.stem: In risk analysis, risk is assessed as:
questions.explanation: Plot each risk on the matrix, then treat by zone: extreme → avoid, high → reduce, medium → transfer, low → accept and monitor.

questions.stem: Buying cyber insurance is an example of which risk treatment?
questions.explanation: Transfer — Note it transfers financial consequence, not reputational damage or legal obligations — a limitation worth naming.

questions.stem: Which treatment applies to a risk rated extreme?
options: Avoid — do not proceed, or change the approach
questions.explanation: Extreme risks are not manageable through controls alone; the activity itself must change.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest control against ransomware in an implementation plan?
options: Daily backups stored on the same server
Immutable, air-gapped offsite backups with tested restores, plus MFA, patching and segmentation
questions.explanation: Ransomware deliberately encrypts reachable backups. An untested backup is not a backup, and a reachable backup is not an offsite one.

questions.stem: Data migration verification should include:
options: Comparing record counts and checksums between source and target, plus spot-checking business-critical fields
questions.explanation: Staged migration with a rollback path is the standard risk treatment — the extract → cleanse → transform → load → verify sequence.

questions.stem: Training should ideally be scheduled:
options: Never — the system should be self-explanatory
Just before go-live, so it is fresh, with ongoing support and updated documentation afterwards
questions.explanation: Under-training is a leading cause of implementation failure. Floor-walking support in week one converts training into competence.

questions.stem: The train-the-trainer / super-user approach is valuable because:
options: It removes the need for documentation
It is the cheapest option in every case
It builds internal capability and provides peer support that scales beyond the vendor's involvement
questions.explanation: Super-users also become advocates, which materially reduces user resistance — a top operational risk at cutover.

questions.stem: Direct (immediate) cutover conversion is characterised by:
options: Lowest cost and fastest, but highest risk — there is no fallback
questions.explanation: Only defensible with total confidence, thorough testing and a documented rollback plan.

questions.stem: Parallel conversion is the safest because:
options: The old system remains available as a fallback and outputs can be cross-validated
questions.explanation: The cost is doubled workload and data entry, staff fatigue, and impossibility where the systems are structurally too different.

questions.stem: A national retailer wants to trial a new POS system in one store before rolling out to 200. This is:
questions.explanation: Pilot — Real-world test at limited scale; pilot users become champions. Risks: delayed benefits, and a pilot site that isn't representative.

questions.stem: Phased conversion introduces:
options: The whole system at one site
The system all at once everywhere
The system module by module or function by function over time
questions.explanation: Risk is contained to one module and training is spread out, at the cost of a long duration and temporary interfaces between old and new.

questions.stem: Justifying a conversion method should weigh:
options: Risk tolerance, cost, organisation size and geography, criticality of the system, and how different the new system is
questions.explanation: A hospital medication system and a staff-room booking tool warrant completely different answers — say why the alternatives are worse.

questions.stem: Interoperability in hardware/software integration means:
options: Different systems can exchange and use data through APIs, agreed formats or middleware
All software comes from one vendor
questions.explanation: Integration should be tested in a staging environment that mirrors production — integration failures found at go-live are the expensive kind.

questions.stem: Verification asks:
options: Are we building the right system?
Are we building the system right — does it meet the specification?
questions.explanation: Validation asks (A). A system can pass verification and fail validation — it does exactly what the spec said, and the spec was wrong.

questions.stem: User acceptance testing primarily achieves:
questions.explanation: Validation — UAT confirms the system meets the users' actual needs and the original success criteria, and is the gateway to sign-off.

questions.stem: In the V-model, unit testing is the counterpart of:
questions.explanation: Detailed design — Integration ↔ high-level design; system testing ↔ system requirements; UAT ↔ problem definition/user needs.

questions.stem: For an "age must be 18–65" rule, which is boundary test data?
questions.explanation: Boundary data sits at and immediately either side of the limits — where most defects live. (A) is normal, (C) and (D) are abnormal.

questions.stem: Abnormal/invalid test data should produce:
options: Graceful rejection with a helpful message
questions.explanation: Include SQL injection strings, emoji, negative numbers and 10,000-character inputs — a crash on any of these is a defect, and often a vulnerability.

questions.stem: Good test data must:
options: Be traceable to a requirement, cover every path and rule, and have a documented expected result
questions.explanation: Without a documented expected result there is nothing to compare the actual result against — you are just running the software, not testing it.

questions.stem: Using live data for testing carries which risk?
options: Privacy exposure and possible corruption of production data
questions.explanation: Use a de-identified copy in a sandbox — never production. Simulated data is safe and lets you construct edge cases deliberately, but may not reflect real messiness.

questions.stem: Regression testing exists to:
options: Re-run existing tests after a change to confirm nothing previously working has broken
questions.explanation: It is the reason automated test suites pay for themselves — manual regression becomes impossible as a system grows.

questions.stem: Stress testing differs from load testing because it:
options: Pushes the system beyond its breaking point to observe how it fails
questions.explanation: What matters is whether failure is graceful (queue, shed load, clear message) or catastrophic (data loss, corruption).

questions.stem: Integration testing verifies that:
options: Modules and external systems exchange data correctly
questions.explanation: Interfaces are where assumptions differ between teams — hence the disproportionate defect density at integration points.

questions.stem: Recovery/disaster testing confirms that:
options: Data can be restored from backup and integrity is preserved after a failure or failover
questions.explanation: This is where "we have backups" becomes "we have restorable backups", and where RPO/RTO targets are actually validated.

questions.stem: Trialling the operation and maintenance documentation properly requires:
options: Someone other than the author to follow it and complete real tasks
questions.explanation: The author cannot detect their own assumed knowledge. Also check currency, accuracy of screenshots, and that documented error messages match the system's actual ones.

questions.stem: Adaptive maintenance responds to:
options: A changed environment — new OS, new legislation, new integrations
A request for a new feature
questions.explanation: Corrective = fix defects, adaptive = respond to environmental change, perfective = improve/enhance, preventive = refactor and patch before problems occur.

questions.stem: Refactoring code and updating dependencies before problems occur is:
questions.explanation: Preventive — It is the maintenance category most often cut from budgets and most reliably regretted.

questions.stem: Reviewing implementation impact across "relevant environments" should cover:
options: Technical, organisational, user/customer, financial, legal/ethical and environmental impacts
questions.explanation: Naming all six domains structures an extended response and demonstrates systems thinking.

questions.stem: A traceability matrix links:
options: Each requirement to its test and result
questions.explanation: It is the direct evidence for the "functionality" criterion — every requirement demonstrably tested and passed.

questions.stem: Which is a measurable evaluation criterion?
options: "Booking handling time reduced from 6 minutes to under 1 minute; double-booking rate 0%"
questions.explanation: Evaluation must return to the measurable success criteria set in the problem definition — that loop closing is what earns marks in an evaluate question.

questions.stem: The correct structure for a strong evaluation answer is:
options: State the criterion → state the evidence → make a judgement → note the limitation → recommend an improvement
questions.explanation: Description without judgement is the single most common way to lose marks on an 8-mark evaluation question.

questions.stem: Which artefact best communicates a completed system to maintainers?
options: Technical documentation with DFDs, ERD, data dictionary, commented code and API docs
questions.explanation: Match the artefact to the audience: executives → concise presentation with benefits, cost and risk; end users → training and quick-reference guides; public → infographic or demo video.

questions.stem: A client demands three extra features mid-build with no change to deadline or budget. The best professional response is:
options: Assess and document the time and cost impact, present the trade-off options (extend, re-prioritise via MoSCoW, or defer), and obtain written agreement
Deliver the features and reduce testing
questions.explanation: Change control makes the trade-off visible and keeps the decision with the client. (D) is how projects fail quietly.

questions.stem: A project is running two weeks behind on a task not on the critical path. The correct response is:
options: Check whether the delay exceeds the task's float; if not, the end date is unaffected but monitor closely
Add staff to the critical path
questions.explanation: Float is exactly the slack a non-critical task has. Consuming all of it, however, promotes the task onto the critical path.

questions.stem: A hospital is replacing its medication management system. The most defensible conversion method is:
options: Parallel or carefully staged phased conversion, because the consequence of failure is patient harm
questions.explanation: Criticality dominates the decision. The cost of running both systems is trivially small compared with the consequence of a medication error.

questions.stem: A team adopts agile but the client is unavailable for feedback. The likely outcome is:
options: Agile works better without client input
The main benefit — continuous validated feedback — is lost, and the team effectively builds on assumptions in short bursts
questions.explanation: Method selection must account for the client's capacity, not just the team's preference. If the client cannot engage, that is an argument for a more structured approach.

questions.stem: A system passes all unit and integration tests but users report it does not solve their problem. This indicates:
options: A validation failure — the specification did not reflect the real need
questions.explanation: Trace it back to the identifying-and-defining phase: inadequate empathise/define work, or requirements gathered from managers rather than actual users.

questions.stem: The best evidence for EC-12-09 (recording management and evaluating development) is:
options: A dated process diary with justified decisions, alongside the Gantt chart showing planned versus actual, and a budget tracking estimated versus actual
questions.explanation: Planned versus actual, on both time and cost, is the core evidence of managed development rather than development that merely happened.

questions.stem: A prototype receives enthusiastic feedback and the client assumes the project is nearly finished. The best mitigation is:
options: Set expectations explicitly — state what is simulated versus built, and use deliberately low-fidelity visuals early on
Hide the prototype from the client
questions.explanation: Low-fidelity wireframes invite critique of structure; high-fidelity mockups invite critique of colour — and create false impressions of progress.

questions.stem: A team wants to skip documentation to hit a deadline. The strongest counter-argument is:
options: Documentation is legally required in all cases
Maintenance is the largest lifetime cost, and undocumented systems create key-person dependency and expensive rework
Documentation makes the code run faster
questions.explanation: The saving is realised this month; the cost is paid every month afterwards.

questions.stem: Which risk category does "the lead developer resigns mid-project" belong to, and what is the best treatment?
options: Project; treat by cross-training, documentation and knowledge sharing
questions.explanation: Key-person dependency is a project risk. Reducing it is a design decision about how the team works, not an insurance purchase.

questions.stem: A new system will change staff workflows significantly. The greatest operational risk is:
options: User resistance and insufficient training causing business disruption at cutover
questions.explanation: Treated with change management, early involvement of affected staff, super-users, timely training and parallel conversion.

questions.stem: The strongest reason to conduct a post-implementation review is:
options: To measure achievement against the original success criteria and capture lessons that improve the next project
questions.explanation: It is scheduled in the implementation plan, with a date, before go-live — otherwise it never happens.

questions.stem: A client asks for a system in 6 weeks that realistically takes 16. The best response is:
options: Present the evidence-based estimate with the WBS, then offer a reduced-scope MVP achievable in 6 weeks with a phased roadmap for the remainder
questions.explanation: Negotiating scope rather than compressing quality is the professional response, and it maps directly to MoSCoW prioritisation.

questions.stem: In a project using outsourced development, the most important contractual protections are:
options: IP ownership, data security and location obligations, SLAs, acceptance criteria and exit/transition arrangements
questions.explanation: Exit arrangements are the most commonly omitted and most consequential — vendor lock-in is realised at the moment you try to leave.

questions.stem: Which best demonstrates ongoing evaluation during development rather than evaluation at the end?
options: A final report submitted after go-live
Diary entries at each iteration assessing progress against the criteria and recording what changed as a result
questions.explanation: Ongoing evaluation must visibly change something — evaluation that never alters a decision is documentation, not evaluation.

questions.stem: A system meets every specification but users still make frequent errors. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Blame the users and add more training
Conduct usability testing to locate the design causes, then modify the design under change control and regression-test
questions.explanation: Persistent user error is usually a design signal, not a user deficiency. "Error prevention over error messages" is the relevant heuristic.

questions.stem: The strongest justification for choosing prototyping for a customer-facing booking interface is:
options: It removes the need for testing
The requirements are UI-heavy and partly unarticulated, so users reacting to a tangible model elicits requirements interviews would miss
questions.explanation: Justify by matching the approach's strength to the project's specific uncertainty — and say why waterfall (requirements not stable) and end-user (customer-facing, needs security) are worse here.

questions.stem: During cutover, the new system fails and the business cannot process orders. The critical omission was most likely:
options: A documented rollback plan and go/no-go criteria
questions.explanation: Every implementation plan needs defined go/no-go criteria and a tested path back to the previous state.

questions.stem: Which combination of evidence best supports a claim that a project was cost-effective?
options: Actual versus budgeted cost, plus quantified benefit (labour hours saved, error reduction, revenue effect) and a payback period
questions.explanation: Cost-effectiveness is a ratio — it needs both sides quantified, and ongoing operating costs included in the denominator.

questions.stem: A project's Gantt chart shows all tasks at 100% complete but UAT has not begun. This most likely indicates:
options: The critical path was too short
The plan omitted testing and evaluation activities, or progress is being reported inaccurately
questions.explanation: Testing must be planned from the start as scheduled work with duration and owners — not treated as something that happens after "the work".

questions.stem: The most defensible reason to choose direct cutover for a small internal staff-room booking tool is:
options: Consequence of failure is low, the system is simple, and parallel running would cost more than the risk it removes
questions.explanation: Right-sizing the method to the risk is the judgement being tested — the same reasoning that rules direct cutover out for a hospital.

questions.stem: An enterprise wants to measure whether a new system improved user experience. The strongest method set is:
options: Pre/post task-completion rate, time on task, error rate and SUS score, with usability testing to explain the numbers
questions.explanation: Quantitative measures show whether it improved; observation explains why. Baseline measurement before deployment is essential.

questions.stem: In communicating results to a non-technical client, the most effective approach is:
options: Lead with the outcome against their stated criteria, use visuals to carry the argument, avoid unexplained jargon, and provide a one-page summary
questions.explanation: EC-12-11 is assessed on fitting the communication to the audience — the client cares whether the 6-minute booking is now 50 seconds.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the relationship between the four project phases?
options: They are strictly sequential and never revisited
They are iterative — testing and evaluation findings feed back into defining, planning and producing, with the process diary and ongoing evaluation running across all four
questions.explanation: The feedback arrows are the point of the diagram. Treating the phases as a one-way street is precisely the waterfall failure mode the syllabus is warning about.
